title: sliding-window-prefetch-reservation-and-batch-aware-token-controller
author: Samir Patel
description:
Motivation: Paged KV cache pinning and the block allocator currently use coarse reservation strategies that either over-reserve under bursty hot prefixes or under-provision when access patterns shift quickly. This PR introduces a sliding-window reservation controller paired with a lightweight prefetch budget allocator and batch-aware token controller to reduce unnecessary pinning and improve steady-state p99 latency under mixed workloads. The design targets three problems: (1) reduce transient over-reservation that inflates memory residency and increases GC churn; (2) prefetch only when upstream batch pressure indicates likely continuation (continuous batching aware); (3) provide a lockless fast-path for token allocation under the common case.

Design summary: The new controller maintains a compact sliding window per-pool (default window 512 requests) that tracks recent hit/miss patterns and allocation hold-times. From that window it derives a dynamic reservation target (reservations are maintained in fractional tokens) that scales up aggressively on sustained hit streaks and decays conservatively when access becomes sparse. A separate prefetch budget module consumes a small portion of the reservation token stream to issue non-blocking prefetches; prefetches are gated by the batch size and current scheduler latency headroom so we avoid dooming low-latency requests for speculative work. To avoid contention on hot paths we implemented a lockless token counter using atomic fetch_add/fetch_sub with an optimistic local-cache fast-path (per-worker token shadow) and slowpath reconciliation under heavy contention.

Implementation highlights:
- src/kv/prefetch/sliding_window_controller.cc / .h: new controller that computes reservation targets from an exponential-decayed histogram and weighted recent-latency samples.
- src/kv/allocator/token_ring.cc: lockless token ring allocator with per-worker shadow caches and a compact serialization for slowpath reconciliation.
- src/serving/scheduler/batch_aware_gate.cc: gate that exposes batch pressure and headroom metrics to the prefetch budget module via an internal API.
- tests/kv/bench/sliding_window_stress_test.cc: microbench stress harness that replays production traces with configurable hotset churn and verifies no regression in allocation throughput.
- docs/architecture/paged-kv-sliding-reservation.md: high-level design doc and rollout guidance.

Benchmarks: Microbench harness run on g5.2x (8xV100-equivalent) and internal A100-80GB perf cluster with a mixed synthetic trace (70% read, 25% short-gen, 5% long-gen) produced the following median results across three 30-minute runs: p99 latency reduced by 9-15% for read-heavy workloads and 5-9% for mixed workloads; end-to-end token cost per request improved by 8-12% due to reduced redundant residency and fewer eviction-triggered reloads. Under extreme churn workloads the sliding-window reduced tail allocation stalls by ~25% relative to the baseline reservoir.

Safety and fallbacks: The controller supports a conservative safe-mode (disabled by default for canary) which pins a minimum reservation equal to the old static heuristic. We also added metrics and alerts for "prefetch-failure-rate" and "reservation-thrashing" to detect pathological cases. If the controller observes sustained elevation in eviction cycles it can throttle prefetches or revert to the static allocator for that pool.

Testing and validation: Unit tests for token semantics, race detection tests (TSan), and a long-running soak (72h) on a staging cluster. One CI integration test initially flaked (tests/integration/kv_integration_test) due to a timing assumption in a test fixture; this was fixed by converting to time-bounded waits and the pipeline was re-run. Performance runs used the internal perf-canary harness and were validated with tracing (NVTX spans) and heap snapshots to measure effective residency.

Rollout plan: Canary on 5% of traffic for two days (canary config in rollout/canaries/2026-02-prefetch.json) then a 25% ramp with automated heuristics checking the metrics above. If any of the reserved alarms fire, the canary controller will automatically disable the new controller for the affected pool.

Docs and Ops: Added an ops runbook and an operable admin flag (runtime.flags.kv_sliding_reservation) in the console for quick toggle. The design doc lists tuning knobs: window_size, growth_factor, decay_half_life, prefetch_budget_ratio, min_reservation.

Checklist: Implemented feature + tests, docs updated, perf validated, rollout configured, canary controls + metrics added.

review_comments: Priya Ramesh: Nice design. Two questions: (1) can you explain how the window size interacts with very bursty clients? (2) can we make prefetch_budget_ratio configurable at runtime?

Author (Samir Patel): For bursty clients the exponential decay ensures the target grows quickly on sustained hits; we also added an explicit cap to avoid runaway. prefetch_budget_ratio is an ops flag and is editable from the console — documented in the ops runbook.
Liam O'Connor: Token_ring slowpath looks good, but please add comments clarifying ABA avoidance; also add a TSan-only stress that toggles workers to force reconciliation.
Author: Added ABA comment and the TSan stress test in tests/kv/unit/token_ring_tsan_toggle_test.cc. Also wired the test under CI to run in TSan job.
Ming Zhao: Observability looks thin for the case where reservation decays too fast and causes churn. Can we add an explicit metric reservation_decay_count and an alert burn-in?
Author: Added 'kv.reservation_decay.count' and an alert rule in ops/alerts/kvcache.alerts.yaml. Added note to runbook to increase decay_half_life if the alert triggers.
